money_at_stake.rationale: Two independent, dated estimates of the whole reconstruction bill converge in the same range: Nepal's own Finance Minister put the initial figure at USD 4-5bn, and a separate, unrelated estimate from a Nepali businessman also landed at 'at least USD 5bn'. A third, sector-specific figure (hydropower losses in the hundreds of billions of rupees, or 25-30% of affected project cost per the independent power producers' association) sits inside that headline total rather than adding to it. Band is B1_10, not THIN, because $4-5bn clears $1bn several times over; not B10_100 because two converging headline sources cap it well under $10bn and the Finance Minister's own framing (per the fetched Star-Advertiser piece) puts this beneath Nepal's 2015 earthquake reconstruction, itself reported around $9bn. This is the CAND record's own occurrence: a discrete flash-flood and glacial-outburst disaster (kind HAPPENED) that began 2026-08-26, not the separate, already-signaled Motuo/Yarlung-Tsangpo mega-dam construction project the candidate's own text loosely associates it with (see notes).

public_reach.rationale: Split, with a large state/unlisted share but a genuinely listed set on both sides of the ledger, which is a stronger, more concrete public-reach signal than a purely narrative one. On the damage side, Nepal Stock Exchange-listed hydropower and non-life insurance names posted real, dated share-price and index declines across the two trading sessions immediately following the flood (hydropower index down 104.33 points Wednesday and 19.78 points Thursday; non-life insurance index down 404.05 points Wednesday, 201.81 points Thursday, a 3.90 percent move; Rasuwagadhi Hydropower down 15 percent Wednesday and 8.38 percent Thursday; Chilime Hydropower down 10.12 percent Wednesday and 5.15 percent Thursday), tied directly to this occurrence. Nepal's energy ministry separately reports nine operational hydropower projects across two districts plus a 25-megawatt solar plant damaged, roughly 8 percent of national generation capacity, with a further five under-construction hydropower projects (390 MW combined) also hit. On the spend side, the single largest identified reconstruction piece (the Gyirong border-crossing rebuild) is expected to draw Chinese state-owned engineering firms, and the bulk of near-term financing is government-to-multilateral (Nepal's own budget, ADB, World Bank, bilateral aid), not a listed-issuer channel. A secondary, contested opportunity for internationally listed EPC firms exists via multilateral-procurement channels, with Larsen & Toubro singled out as carrying the most direct contract exposure and AECOM/Fluor framed as longer-dated, procurement-timeline-contingent plays; this channel is explicitly framed as competing with, not replacing, the state-directed Gyirong piece. Scored 40 rather than 60 because the state/multilateral channel appears to carry the larger share of the headline pool; scored 40 rather than 15 because real, currently-pricing listed exposure exists on the domestic side, some of it in the same named companies whose plants were damaged, and a real contract-competition channel exists on the international side.

capture_odds.rationale: The dominant, evidenced money movement right now is destruction, not capture: the listed Nepali hydropower and insurance names in scope are recording share-price declines, which is a cost borne, not a profit earned. The reconstruction-spend side that could convert into revenue for a listed issuer is procurement-driven and multilateral (World Bank and ADB emergency procurement portals, formal requests for proposals still pending), a structure that runs toward thin-margin, competitively-bid work rather than qualification-locked pricing power, and the single largest identified piece (the Gyirong crossing) is expected to draw a Chinese state-owned builder, which by definition does not stick as profit to a listed issuer. Scored 30, above the commodity/regulated floor of 15, because a real, if competitive, contract-win channel exists for internationally listed EPC firms (Larsen & Toubro named as carrying the most direct exposure) once financing is confirmed; not scored at 40 or above because no contract has yet been awarded to any listed name, the process is still at the 'monitor for the first formal requests for proposals' stage, and multilateral tendering both compresses margins and can bypass the largest single piece entirely.

timing_fit.rationale: Funding intent and damage assessment are moving now and squarely inside the 2-5 year horizon: Nepal's Finance Minister put a dollar estimate on the table within days of the event (flood onset 2026-08-26, Finance Minister quote published 2026-08-29), and multilateral and bilateral partners (India, China, the US, the World Bank) were offering support the same day the disaster was first reported (2026-08-26). Not scored 85+ because the government's own number is explicitly provisional ('just an estimate'), no contract has yet been awarded to any listed name, and the process is still at the pre-RFP monitoring stage per the capture_odds evidence; the nearest comparable, Nepal's 2015 earthquake reconstruction, ran over several years past its initial estimates (Star-Advertiser reports its cost near $9bn against this event's $4-5bn), so company-level contract revenue plausibly lands 1 to 4 years out rather than being committed today. That range sits comfortably inside this repo's 2-5 year window, which is why this scores well above the 30 'slipping past it' anchor.

notes.text: CAND-20260829-02 carries no occurrence block (no kind/anchor_date/window), unlike a SIG- card; every candidate row in data/radar/candidates.json is shaped this way, and tools/check_impact.py accordingly only requires a CAND- occurrence_id to resolve in that file, not an anchor_date match. I anchored to the flash flood's own dated start (2026-08-26, confirmed by multiple outlets) rather than the candidate's 2026-08-29 triage date.

Second and more important finding: this occurrence is not, on the evidence, the same thing as the Motuo/Yarlung-Tsangpo mega-dam project this candidate's own 'why' field associates it with (SIG-20260828-02, chain tibet-mega-dam). The disaster driving every figure in this appraisal is a glacial-outburst flash flood on Nepal's Bhotekoshi/Trishuli river systems, a different river and a different country's infrastructure from the Motuo dam site on the Yarlung Tsangpo. It is a real, large, well-evidenced occurrence in its own right (734+ confirmed dead in Nepal alone as of 2026-08-30 per multiple outlets, a government-estimated USD 4-5bn rebuild), with its own money profile independent of the mega-dam chain. Nell filed it AMBIENT on the reasoning that 'that chain already exists,' which this appraisal's evidence does not support: the two occurrences share a headline keyword ('Tibet'/'dam'/'barrier lake') but not a chain. This is a finding for radar to weigh, not a signal card I am writing or a dismissal I am making.
